transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. What brings you here today?

I… I’m here because I keep noticing my face in lesson videos. One side looks crooked to me, kind of swollen, and once I see it I can’t stop thinking that the students, parents, even other staff are staring at that instead of listening to what I’m saying.
Do you feel that others are noticing or judging this facial asymmetry in a negative way?

Yes… I do. I know I can’t really prove it, but when I see that side of my face looking crooked or swollen in the lesson videos, it feels like that’s what everyone is noticing. Like the students, parents, staff… they’re looking at that, not listening to me.
Has this concern about your facial appearance affected your ability to teach or interact with students, parents, or coworkers?

Yeah… it has. I’m not keeping up like I used to.

Lesson planning takes me forever and a lot of it just doesn’t get finished on time. I’ve fallen behind with mentoring and coaching basketball too. Admin has started writing things down—missed deadlines, coverage problems. I’m… worried I might lose my job if it keeps going.
How much time do you spend each day thinking about the way your face looks, and does it interfere with other parts of your life like teaching, sleeping, or being with family and friends?

It’s… a lot of the day. I don’t really keep count.

Once I see my face in those lesson videos, that one side looking crooked or kind of swollen, it just stays in my head. Then I start thinking the students, parents, staff… everyone must be staring at it instead of listening to me. It makes it hard to focus on teaching.
Do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly—like checking your face in mirrors, taking videos, or asking others how you look—to try to fix or confirm how your face appears?

Yeah… I do some of that.

Before I post a recorded lesson or if I have to join a parent conference, I’ll keep adjusting the camera angle and replaying little clips. Sometimes I cover part of my face with my hand to see if it looks less… off. And then I’ll re-record it again.

It can take a long time. I’ve missed prep because of it, and sometimes I’m late getting to class.
Outside of your teaching responsibilities, does this concern about your face make it hard for you to be around friends or family, or does it affect your sleep?

I’m not really sure. I mean… I don’t go out much lately, but I haven’t really thought about whether that’s because of my face or just being tired.

Sleep is… not great sometimes, but I don’t know if it’s because of that specifically.
Has your concern about your face made it hard for you to spend time with friends or family, or caused you to avoid social situations altogether?

I don’t know… maybe a little. I’ve been keeping to myself more, but I can’t really say it’s only because of my face.

Sometimes it just feels easier not to deal with people. That’s about all I can say.

Outside of your concerns about your face affecting your teaching, have you found yourself avoiding social situations, withdrawing from others, or experiencing significant distress in your personal life because of how you perceive your face?

I’m… not sure. I don’t really track it that way.

I do avoid some things, I guess, but I can’t say for certain it’s because of my face. It’s more like I just don’t feel up to being around people sometimes. That’s all I really know.
Have you ever avoided seeing friends, family, or going out in public because you were too worried about how that side of your face looked?

I don’t know if I’d put it that strongly. I mean… I’ve skipped things before, but I’m not sure I can say it was exactly because of that.

Sometimes I just don’t feel like being seen, I guess. But… yeah, I don’t really know.
Can you think of a time when you avoided being with friends, family, or going out in public specifically because you were overly concerned about how your face looked?
I… I can’t really think of a specific time like that. I mean, I’ve avoided things before, but saying it was definitely because of my face feels… I don’t know. I’m not sure.
Have you ever felt so upset or self-conscious about that side of your face that you couldn’t bring yourself to be with people, even those you care about?

I don’t… I don’t know. Maybe sometimes I’ve felt too self-conscious to deal with people, but I can’t really say it like that for sure.

It’s just… sometimes I’d rather not be around anyone. That’s about all I can say.
Do you feel that your concern about your face causes you significant distress or makes it hard for you to function in your personal life or relationships?

Yeah… I guess it does. More than I like admitting.

Work’s been… slipping. I’m behind on lesson plans, mentoring stuff, even basketball coaching things I’m supposed to keep up with. A lot of it just doesn’t get finished on time anymore.

Admin has started writing down missed deadlines and coverage issues, so… I’m worried I might be close to losing my job.
Has your concern about your face ever made you feel so upset or embarrassed that you couldn't bring yourself to be around people, even those close to you?

I… I’m not really sure how to answer that.

I’ve avoided people at times, yeah, but saying it was because of that exactly… I don’t know. I don’t really want to make it sound bigger than it is.
Can you describe how your concern about your face has affected your personal relationships or daily life outside of teaching?

I’m not sure I can describe it very well.

Outside of teaching… I guess I keep more to myself than I used to. I don’t always feel like going out or answering messages. But I don’t know how much of that is… my face specifically, or just me being tired of dealing with things.

It’s affected things some, yeah. I just don’t really know how to explain it.

Can you think of any specific times when your concern about your face caused you to pull away from someone close to you, like a friend or family member, or made it hard to take part in personal relationships?

I don’t know… not a specific time, no.

I mean, I probably have pulled back sometimes, but I can’t really point to one moment and say, “that was because of my face.” It’s more like I just don’t feel up to dealing with people, and then I keep things short or don’t go.

But… I’m not sure.
Has your concern about your face ever caused problems in your personal relationships, like arguments, distance from others, or difficulty connecting with people close to you?

I don’t really know. Maybe some distance, I guess, but I couldn’t say for sure it’s because of my face.

I haven’t had big arguments about it or anything. I just… sometimes don’t feel like talking much, and people probably notice that. That’s all I can really say.

Do you find yourself doing things like checking your face in mirrors, covering part of it, or adjusting lighting when you're not preparing for a lesson or meeting—like when you're at home or out in public?

Yeah… I do some of that.

Mostly when there’s a recorded lesson or a parent conference. I’ll keep changing the camera angle, replaying clips, putting my hand near part of my face… sometimes I end up re-recording the whole thing. It can take a lot longer than it should, and then I’m behind on prep or late getting to class.
Outside of teaching, have you ever felt so distressed about that side of your face that it affected your ability to engage in personal relationships or enjoy time with friends and family?

I’m not really sure. I don’t think I can point to something outside work where it clearly stopped me from being with people.

I mean, sometimes I’m not in the mood to see anyone, but… I don’t know if that’s because of my face or just me being tired or wanting to be left alone.
Have you ever felt so self-conscious about your face that you avoided spending time with someone close to you, even if it meant disappointing them or causing some distance between you?

I don’t know. Maybe I’ve been a bit withdrawn sometimes, but I can’t really say I avoided someone close just because of my face.

I wouldn’t want to make it sound bigger than it is. I just… keep to myself sometimes.

Have your concerns about the way your face looks ever caused you significant distress or made it hard for you to function in areas of your life outside of teaching, like being with friends, family, or enjoying activities you used to like?

I’m… not sure I can say that.

Outside of teaching, I don’t really have a clear example where it’s stopped me doing something. I might avoid things sometimes, but I don’t know if that’s because of my face or just not feeling up to it.
